These applications coming on for admission this day, the court passed the following:
 ORDER
By this common order, MCRC No.50654/2020 filed by Smt. Jyoti Nayak shall also be considered.

2. Both the applications have been filed under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. for quashment of FIR in Crime No.643/2020 registered at Police Station Civil Lines, Chhatarpur for offence under Sections 498-A of IPC and under Section 3/4 of Dowry Prohibition Act.

3. The facts necessary for disposal of both the applications in short are that applicants Asish Mishra & Smt. Chandraprabha are husband and mother-in-law of complainant Smt. Madhulika Mishra whereas Smt. Jyoti Nayak is the sister-in-law of complainant Smt. Madhulika Mishra.
Complainant lodged an FIR for offence under Section 498A of IPC and under Section 3/4 of Dowry Prohibition Act.
In the FIR it was alleged that respondent No.2 got married to applicant No.1 Asish Mishra on 21.01.2004 as per Hindu rites and rituals.
She was kept properly in her matrimonial house for one year and from thereafter her in-laws started demanding Rs.5,00,000/- on the ground that her father has not given anything in the dowry.
This fact was narrated by her to her father.
After the birth of her first daughter, her father somehow gave Rs.2,00,000/-.
After the birth of her first daughter, her in-laws started passing taunts and also started demanding money.
Her in-laws started harassing her mentally.
However, she continued to tolerate the same.
After the birth of second daughter in the year 2018 her in-laws started harassing her physically and mentally.
On 18.05.2020 her husband insisted that she should go back to her parental home alongwith her daughters and she should come back only with an amount of Rs.50,00,000/-.

Thereafter, she narrated the entire incident to her Jyoti Nayak vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 10 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/95921017/
2 father on phone and accordingly, she went back to Chhatarpur alongwith her father.

sentences.text: On 13.07.2020 at about 4 p.m. her husband and mother-in-law came to her parental home at Chhatarpur and demanded Rs.50,00,000/- and instructed that she can come in case if amount of Rs.50,00,000/- is given, otherwise she should continue to stay back in her parental home and both her daughters were forcibly taken away by her husband.
She was tolerating the mental harassment.
She also sent a message through Parivar Paramarsh Kendra for reconciliation but her husband did not join and accordingly, on 06.11.2020 FIR was lodged.

4. From plain reading of FIR it is clear that there is not a single whisper of allegation against Jyoti Nayak, although there are allegations of demand of dowry and mental and physical cruelty by her husband Asish Mishra and her mother-in-law Smt. Chandraprabha Mishra.

The statement of complainant was recorded under Section 161 of Cr.P.C. in which she has stated that for one year after her marriage she was kept properly but thereafter her husband Asish Mishra, sister-in-law Jyoti and mother-in-law Chandraprabha started scolding that her father has not given anything in dowry, therefore, she should bring an amount of Rs.5,00,000/- from her father.
This fact was narrated by her to her father and brother Madhur Mishra.
When she gave birth to her first girl child then her father and brother gave an amount of Rs.2,00,000/-.

It was further alleged that her mother-in-law, sister-in-law and husband started alleging that she has not given birth to a child (as mentioned in the statement itself) and started scolding her and also started making further demand of money and her husband, mother-in-law and sister-in-law started harassing her mentally.
She gave birth to second child in the year 2008 and her in-laws are harassing her mentally and physically.
On 18.05.2020 her husband insisted that she should go back to her parental home alongwith both of her daughters and should come back with an amount of Rs.50,00,000/-.
This fact was narrated by her to her father on phone and accordingly, she went back to Chhatarpur alongwith her father.
The entire incident was narrated to her neighbour Nilesh S/o Krishna Gopal Dubey.

On 13.07.2020 at about 04:00 p.m. her husband and mother-in-law Chandraprabha came to her parental home in Chhatarpur and stated that she should accompany them after taking Rs.50,00,000/- from her father otherwise she should stay back in her parental home and forcibly took away both of her daughters.
She made a complaint to Mahila Paramarsh Kendra but her husband did not respond to notice sent by Mahila Paramarsh Kendra and accordingly, FIR was lodged.

5. Challenging the FIR lodged against the husband and mother-in- law, it is submitted by counsel for applicants that FIR was lodged after 16 years of marriage and prior thereto no complaint was made to police which indicates that FIR has been lodged on false ground.
6.

Considered the submissions made by counsel for applicants Asish Mishra and Smt.
Chandraprabha Mishra.

7. If FIR as well as statement of complainant recorded under Section 161 of Cr.P.C. are considered,
then it is clear that there are allegations of demand of dowry and physical or mental cruelty against the husband and mother-in-law.

sentences.text: We have gone through the FIR and the criminal complaint.
In the FIR, the appellants have not been named and in the criminal complaint they have been named without attributing any specific role to them.
The relationship of the appellants with the husband of the complainant is distant.

In Kans Raj v. State of Punjab [Kans Raj v.
State of Punjab, (2000) 5 SCC 207 : 2000 SCC (Cri) 935 : (2000) 3 SCR 662] it was observed (SCC p. 217, para 5):
"5. ... A tendency has, however, developed for roping in all relations of the in- laws of the deceased wives in the matters of dowry deaths which, if not discouraged, is likely to affect the case of the prosecution even against the real culprits.

State of Punjab, (2000) 5 SCC 207 : 2000 SCC (Cri) 935 : (2000) 3 SCR 662]

sentences.text: In their overenthusiasm and anxiety to seek conviction for maximum people, the parents of the deceased have been found to be making efforts for involving other relations which ultimately weaken the case of the prosecution even against the real accused as appears to have happened in the instant case."
The Court has, thus, to be careful in summoning distant relatives without there being specific material.

Only the husband, his parents or at best close family members may be expected to demand dowry or to harass the wife but not distant relations, unless there is tangible material to support allegations made against such distant relations.
Mere naming of distant relations is not enough to summon them in the absence of any specific role and material to support such role.
9. The parameters for quashing proceedings in a criminal complaint are well known.

If there are triable issues, the Court is not expected to go into the veracity of the rival versions but where on the face of it, the criminal proceedings are abuse of Court's process, quashing jurisdiction can be exercised.
Reference may be made to K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar [K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar, (2000) 8 SCC 547 : 2001 SCC (Cri) 27] ,

14. From a reading of the complaint, it cannot be held that even if the allegations are taken as proved no case is made out.
There are allegations against Respondent 2 and his parents for harassing the complainant which forced her to leave the matrimonial home.
Even now she continues to be separated from the matrimonial home as she apprehends lack of security and safety and proper environment in the matrimonial home.
The question whether the appellant has in fact been harassed and treated with cruelty is a matter of trial but at this stage, it cannot be said that no case is made out.

Thus, quashing of proceedings before the trial is not permissible."
8.
So far as delay in lodging the FIR is concerned, it is suffice to mention here that delay in lodging the FIR by itself cannot be a ground to quash the proceedings.

The Supreme Court in the case of Mohammad Wajid and another vs. State of U.P. and others, reported in AIR 2023 SC 3784 has held that delay in registration of FIR, by itself cannot be a ground for quashing of FIR.

entities.text: Mohammad Wajid and another vs. State of U.P. and others, reported in AIR 2023 SC 3784
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, it is clear that merely because according to applicants there is delay in lodging the FIR by itself is not sufficient to quash the same.
9. However, it is also well known fact that a girl after suffering at the hands of her in-laws will not generally lodge the FIR immediately but will make every attempt to save her marital life.
If respondent No.2 did not lodge the FIR immediately then that by itself would not be sufficient for this Court to draw an inference that allegations made in the FIR are false and baseless.

10. Under these circumstances, this Court is of considered opinion that so far as allegations made against the applicants Asish Mishra and Smt. Chandraprabha are concerned, they are sufficient for their prosecution under Section 498A of IPC and under Section 3/4 of Dowry Prohibition Act.

sentences.text: Smt. Jyoti Nayak is the sister-in-law of respondent No.2.
FIR lodged by respondent No.2 and her statement recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C. has already been reproduced.
In the FIR no allegation whatsoever has been made against sister-in-law Smt. Jyoti Nayak.

Although counsel for complainant tried to convince this Court by drawing the attention towards the subject of written complaint in which it was mentioned that complaint is being made with regard to cruelty committed by her husband, mother-in-law and sister-in-law but after reading out the entire FIR it is fairly conceded by Shri Mishra that there are no allegations against Smt. Jyoti Nayak.

12. Although counsel for respondent No.2 tried to convince this Court by submitting that in the FIR the word "in-laws" has been mentioned which would include the applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak but this Court is of considered opinion that in the penal cases this Court cannot enlarge the scope of word "in-laws" by including each and every person, who may be related to husband of complainant.

Thus,
it is clear that no allegation whatsoever was made by respondent No.2 against the applicant Smt.
Jyoti Nayak in the FIR at all.

13. So far as statement of respondent No.2 recorded under Section 161 of Cr.P.C. is concerned, this Court would like to consider the law governing the field of prosecution of near and dear relatives of husband of complainant.

14. The Supreme Court in the case of Kans Raj v. State of Punjab, reported in (2000) 5 SCC 207 has held as under:
"In the light of the evidence in the case we find substance in the submission of the learned counsel for the defence that Respondents 3 to 5 were roped in the case only on the ground of being close relations of Respondent 2, the husband of the deceased.

sentences.text: For the fault of the husband, the in-laws or the other relations cannot, in all cases, be held to be involved in the demand of dowry.
In cases where such accusations are made, the overt acts attributed to persons other than the husband are required to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
By mere conjectures and implications such relations cannot be held guilty for the offence relating to dowry deaths.

A tendency has, however, developed for roping in all relations of the in-laws of the deceased wives in the matters of dowry deaths which, if not discouraged, is likely to affect the case of the prosecution even against the real culprits.

In their over enthusiasm and anxiety to seek conviction for maximum people, the parents of the deceased have been found to be making efforts for involving other relations which ultimately weaken the case of the prosecution even against the real accused as appears to have happened in the instant case."

The court has to adopt a pragmatic view and when a girl dies an unnatural death,
allegation of demand of dowry or harassment which follows cannot be weighed in golden scales.
At the same time, omnibus allegation against all family members particularly against the brothers and sisters and other relatives do not stand on the same footing as husband and parents.

In such case, apart from general allegation of demand of dowry, the court has to be satisfied that harassment was also caused by all the named members."

sentences.text: We must, at the outset, state that the High Court's view on jurisdiction meets with our approval and we confirm the view However, after a careful perusal of the FIR and after taking into consideration the attendant circumstances, we are of the opinion that the FIR lodged by respondent 2 insofar as it relates to appellants 1, 2 and 3 deserves to be quashed.
The allegations are extremely general in nature.
No specific role is attributed to each of the appellants.
Respondent 2 has stated that after the marriage, she resided with her husband at Ahmedabad.
It is not clear whether appellants 1, 2 and 3 were residing with them at Ahmedabad.

The marriage took place on 9/7/2002 and respondent 2 left her matrimonial home on 15/2/2003 i.e.
within a period of seven months.
Thereafter, respondent 2 took no steps to file any complaint against the appellants.
Six years after she left the house, the present FIR is lodged making extremely vague and general allegations against appellants 1, 2 and 3.
It is important to remember that appellant 2 is a married sister-in-law.

In our opinion, such extra ordinary delay in lodging the FIR raises grave doubt about the truthfulness of allegations made by respondent 2 against appellants 1, 2 and 3, which are, in any case, general in nature.
We have no doubt that by making such reckless and vague allegations, respondent 2 has tried to rope them in this case along with her husband.
We are of the confirmed opinion that continuation of the criminal proceedings against appellants 1, 2 and 3 pursuant to this FIR is an abuse of process of law.
In the interest of justice, therefore, the FIR deserves to be quashed insofar as it relates to appellants 1, 2 and 3."

17. Thus, it is clear that in order to prosecute the near and dear relatives of husband of complainant,
the allegations must be specific and clear and should not be vague, omnibus and general.

If the statement of respondent No.2 which was recorded under Section 161 of Cr.P.C. is considered, then it is clear that in the first part of the statement a general allegation has been made against the applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak alongwith other in-laws.
However, in the second part of the statement there is no allegation at all against the applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak.

18. Under these circumstances, this Court is of considered opinion that even if statement of respondent No.2 recorded under Section 161 of Cr.P.C. is taken on its face value, the prosecution of applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak is not warranted because allegations are vague, omnibus and general in nature which are not sufficient for prosecution of near and dear relatives of husband of complainant.
Accordingly, FIR as well as charge sheet and consequential proceedings instituted against applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak are hereby quashed.
19. As a consequence thereof, MCRC No.43114/2023 filed by Asish Mishra and Smt. Chandraprabha Mishra is hereby dismissed.

The prosecution of Asish Mishra and Smt. Chandraprabha Mishra for offence under Section 498A of IPC and under Section 3/4 of Dowry Prohibition Act shall continue and MCRC No.50654/2020 filed by Smt. Jyoti Nayak is hereby allowed.

opennyai_summary.facts: Complainant lodged an FIR for offence under Section 498A of IPC and under Section 3/4 of Dowry Prohibition Act.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The Supreme Court in the case of Taramani Parakh Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh and Others reported in (2015) 11 SCC 260 has held as under:-
Jyoti Nayak vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 10 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/95921017/

In Kans Raj v. State of Punjab [Kans Raj v.
State of Punjab, (2000) 5 SCC 207 : 2000 SCC (Cri) 935 : (2000) 3 SCR 662] it was observed (SCC p. 217, para 5):
"5. ... A tendency has, however, developed for roping in all relations of the in- laws of the deceased wives in the matters of dowry deaths which, if not discouraged, is likely to affect the case of the prosecution even against the real culprits.
The Court has, thus, to be careful in summoning distant relatives without there being specific material.
Only the husband, his parents or at best close family members may be expected to demand dowry or to harass the wife but not distant relations, unless there is tangible material to support allegations made against such distant relations.
Mere naming of distant relations is not enough to summon them in the absence of any specific role and material to support such role.
9. The parameters for quashing proceedings in a criminal complaint are well known.
If there are triable issues, the Court is not expected to go into the veracity of the rival versions but where on the face of it, the criminal proceedings are abuse of Court's process, quashing jurisdiction can be exercised.
Reference may be made to K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar [K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar, (2000) 8 SCC 547 : 2001 SCC (Cri) 27] ,
Pepsi Foods Ltd. v. Judicial Magistrate [Pepsi Foods Ltd. v. Judicial Magistrate, (1998) 5 SCC 749 :

If respondent No.2 did not lodge the FIR immediately then that by itself would not be sufficient for this Court to draw an inference that allegations made in the FIR are false and baseless.

17. Thus, it is clear that in order to prosecute the near and dear relatives of husband of complainant,
the allegations must be specific and clear and should not be vague, omnibus and general.
If the statement of respondent No.2 which was recorded under Section 161 of Cr.P.C. is considered, then it is clear that in the first part of the statement a general allegation has been made against the applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak alongwith other in-laws.
However, in the second part of the statement there is no allegation at all against the applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak.
18. Under these circumstances, this Court is of considered opinion that even if statement of respondent No.2 recorded under Section 161 of Cr.P.C. is taken on its face value, the prosecution of applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak is not warranted because allegations are vague, omnibus and general in nature which are not sufficient for prosecution of near and dear relatives of husband of complainant.
opennyai_summary.arguments: 12. Although counsel for respondent No.2 tried to convince this Court by submitting that in the FIR the word "in-laws" has been mentioned which would include the applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak but this Court is of considered opinion that in the penal cases this Court cannot enlarge the scope of word "in-laws" by including each and every person, who may be related to husband of complainant.

Accordingly, FIR as well as charge sheet and consequential proceedings instituted against applicant Smt. Jyoti Nayak are hereby quashed.
